Title: "Location, Location, Location": Effects of Neighborhood and House Attributes on Burglars' Target Selection
Authors: Christophe Vandeviver, Wim Bernasco
Unit_Selection_Rationale: The authors justify their choice of spatial unit size by emphasizing that burglars target individual residences rather than entire neighborhoods. They argue that the appropriate level of aggregation for studying burglary target choice is at the residence level, supported by previous research. The use of "statistical districts" as neighborhoods is based on administrative divisions and is consistent with previous studies. The neighborhood size is small enough to capture local variations but large enough to be meaningful for analysis.
Direct.quote...page: "address coordinates were withheld by Statistics Belgium to comply with privacy regulations." (p. 791)
Data_Limitations:
Use of predefined "statistical districts" as neighborhoods may not align with actual spatial patterns.
- Neighborhood and residence data were not contemporaneous with burglary data.
- Census data lack relevant variables for burglary target selection.
- Scarcity of large-scale residence-level data and difficulty in measuring situational cues.
- Assumptions about burglary trip origins and offender information may not be accurate.
Direct.quote...page.1: "Even in a high-performance computing environment, estimation of a nested logit model on a choice set as large as our dataset... proved to be computationally prohibitive." (p. 794)
Computational_Constraints: The authors mentioned that the nested logit model was computationally prohibitive due to the large dataset size (138,321 residences nested in 193 neighborhoods for each of the 679 burglaries), even with high-performance computing. This forced them to use the less flexible but computationally less demanding conditional logit model.
